before.title: The gradient norm dominates the H-one norm on zero-boundary Sobolev space
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice as declared by the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, and write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $H_0^1(\Omega):=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)$ the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then $H^1(\Omega)$ and its closed subspace $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are complete, the quadratic integral norm is a Hilbert norm (its coordinate $L^2$ inner products satisfy the parallelogram law), and $$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le2L\,\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2\le2L\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega). $$ In particular the gradient seminorm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on $H_0^1$, and the argument needs neither a smooth domain nor a general boundary-trace theorem.
before.strategy: For $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ extend $v$ by zero to the box $(-L,L)^3$ (legitimate because $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$). Along each coordinate line the Newton-Leibniz formula ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]) gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-L}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$; Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $|v|^2\le2L\int_{-L}^{L}|\partial_1v|^2ds$, and integrating in the other coordinates and then in $x_1$ over a length-$2L$ interval gives $\|v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2$, hence the displayed inequality with $2L$ in the first bound. Approximation in the $W^{1,2}$ norm (the definition of $H_0^1$ as a closure, [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) passes both the inequality and the equivalences to all of $H_0^1$ by continuity of the $L^2$ norm; completeness is the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]) restricted to the closed subspace, and the Hilbert-norm claim follows because the $W^{1,2}$ quadratic norm is induced by the coordinate $L^2$ inner products, which satisfy the parallelogram law.
